summary: This standards-track specification lists standard mailbox names for reaching common roles at an organization, so you know where to send a message even without knowing who works there.

plainLanguage.summary: Standard doorbells that every house puts out, so you know where to ring.

questions: what is the postmaster email address
subtitle: The standard addresses, like postmaster and abuse, that every organization on the Internet should answer.

tldr.problem: When something breaks or you need a human at an organization, you often do not know who to write to, and different protocols had grown their own informal conventions.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2142 collects the well-known mailbox names for business functions, network operations, specific Internet services, mailing lists, DNS zones and autonomous systems, and says organizations must support the ones that match services they offer.
tldr.outcome: Anyone can write to postmaster, abuse, support and similar names at a domain and expect them to reach a suitable person. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and notes that flooding such mailboxes becomes easier when everyone uses the same names.

facts.label: Synonyms
facts.value: NEWS for USENET, WWW for WEBMASTER

today: RFC 2142 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so its list of mailbox names is still the specification on record.

sections.title: Rationale and Purpose
sections.content:
Several documents already require or assume mailbox names for reaching the operators of a service. RFC 822 requires a POSTMASTER@domain mailbox on all hosts that have an SMTP server. Other names were de facto standards: USENET@domain for NNTP, WEBMASTER@domain for HTTP, and protocol-independent ones such as ABUSE@domain and TROUBLE@domain.

This memo gathers and specifies the basic set that organizations need. Most organizations will not need all of them, because not every organization runs every associated service. But if a service is offered, its mailbox name must be supported, with delivery to a recipient appropriate for that service or role. Extra names and aliases are not prohibited.
sections.plainLanguage: Some mailbox names, like postmaster, were already used by habit. This document writes them all down in one list so everyone agrees.

sections.title: Where the Names Apply
sections.content:
The scope of a well-known mailbox name is its domain name. Servers accepting mail for a domain must accept and correctly process these names for that domain, even if the server itself does not provide the related service. For example, if an NNTP server advertises the organization's top-level domain in its Path: headers, the mail exchangers for that domain must accept mail to USENET@domain even if they do not serve NNTP.

A host that does not accept mail directly but runs a service with a defined mailbox name must have an MX record set, and the listed mail exchangers must treat the host's domain name as local for that mailbox. This holds even if the advertised domain differs from the host's name, so both USENET@VIX.COM and USENET@DATA.RAMONA.VIX.COM must work in the RFC's example, though they may be delivered to different final places.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule works for the whole address, like a school's main office. Even if the person at the door does not run the lunchroom, they still have to pass your lunchroom question along.

sections.title: Invariants
sections.content:
For well-known names that are not tied to a protocol, only the organization's top-level domain must be valid. If an Internet service provider is COMPANY.COM, then ABUSE@COMPANY.COM must work, even though the customers who cause complaints use hosts like SHELL1.COMPANY.COM. Supporting these names for sub-domains is valid and encouraged.

Mailbox names must be recognized regardless of character case, so POSTMASTER, postmaster and PoStMaStEr all go to the same mailbox. Implementations should consider what senders expect. Sending an automatic acknowledgement is usually helpful, but the RFC cautions against duelling mail robots and the mail loops they create.
sections.plainLanguage: Capital letters do not matter, like how a doorbell rings the same no matter how you press it. And a machine that answers back should be careful not to start an endless chat with another machine.

sections.title: The Well-Known Mailbox Names
sections.content:
The names fall into three groups. Business names (INFO, MARKETING, SALES, SUPPORT) cover line-of-business activity. INFO is often tied to an autoresponder with standard files available. Network operations names (ABUSE, NOC, SECURITY) give customers, providers and others recourse when they have trouble with the organization's Internet service.

Service names are for major protocol services: POSTMASTER for SMTP, HOSTMASTER for DNS, USENET (with synonym NEWS) for NNTP, WEBMASTER (with synonym WWW) for HTTP, UUCP for UUCP and FTP for FTP. The synonyms are included because of their large installed base.
sections.plainLanguage: There are labels for the shop side (sales, support), the trouble side (abuse, security) and the technical side (postmaster, webmaster), so you pick the right door.

sections.title: Lists, DNS and Autonomous Systems
sections.content:
For a mailing list with submission address LIST@DOMAIN, the administrative address LIST-REQUEST@DOMAIN MUST exist, for add and drop requests and other meta-queries. List software such as MajorDomo and Listserv has its own generic mailbox, but that forces participants to know the software in use, which the RFC calls problematic. List-specific -REQUEST names are therefore required whether or not generic software names exist.

In DNS, the SOA record has a field for the zone administrator's mailbox. It must be a simple word without metacharacters such as %, ! or ::, and a mail alias should direct the mail to the right place. It is strongly recommended that HOSTMASTER@domain always be used.

Several Internet registries run mailing lists for Autonomous System contacts, for instance AS3557@RA.NET reached the technical contact for AS 3557 at the time of writing. Since not every AS is registered everywhere, an undeliverable name of this kind is an inconvenience, not an error or a standards violation.
sections.plainLanguage: Every club mailing list needs a helper address for joining and leaving. The DNS zone owner and network owners get their own shared mailboxes too.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The only concern the RFC raises is denial of service. Flooding a mailbox with junk becomes easier once this document is a standard, because more systems will support the same set of mailbox names and attackers will know what to target.
sections.plainLanguage: When everyone knows where the front desk is, a troublemaker knows where to dump junk mail too.

items.label: SMTP
items.desc: Required by RFC 822 on hosts with an SMTP server.

items.label: DNS
items.desc: Strongly recommended as the SOA zone administrator mailbox.
